description: The mahua tree anchors the adivasi year: its fleshy spring flowers are gathered at dawn, sun-dried, and eaten as a naturally sweet snack or worked into laddoos, halwa-style preparations and jaggery-mahua mixes. The dried flowers taste like caramel-raisin; the sweets built on them are increasingly sold by community enterprises and at fairs like Dang Darbar and Devmogra. April–May is gathering season; dried mahua keeps year-round.
season: Flowers gathered March–May; dried products year-round
cultural_note: Mahua is a sacred, economically vital tree in adivasi life. Its fermented use is heritage context — Gujarat is a dry state, and the sweets are the traveller's lane.
